analysis.one_liner: Moves large interstate class action lawsuits into federal court and restricts abusive settlement practices.
analysis.headline: The House passed the bill 253-170 on June 12, 2003, but the Senate never voted on it, and it died when the 108th Congress ended in January 2005.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would move class action lawsuits involving people from multiple states, with more than $5 million at stake, out of state courts and into federal courts. Defendants could move the cases to federal court without everyone's agreement, and losing or winning a decision to treat a case as a class action could be appealed right away, pausing the case while the appeal is decided. It also sets new rules for settlements: courts could no longer approve deals where class members get coupons of little value, end up owing money to the lawyers, or where nearby class members or the class representatives get a bigger share. Supporters framed it as protecting class members from bad settlements and companies from friendly local courts; its main practical effect is to make it easier for companies to move big class actions into federal court.
analysis.who_benefits: Companies facing class action lawsuits over consumer fraud, defective products, or employment practices, because they can move the case into federal court, where class actions are harder to certify and easier to appeal. Class members also get real protections against coupon-only settlements and deals that leave them owing money to their own lawyers.

how_it_helps.text: Courts could not approve a settlement giving class members coupons or other noncash benefits unless a hearing finds the deal is fair, reasonable, and adequate for class members.
Courts could not approve a settlement that leaves any class member with a net loss after paying class counsel's fees, unless nonmonetary benefits outweigh the loss.
Courts could not approve settlements that pay some class members more simply because they live closer to the courthouse, or that give class representatives a larger share than everyone else.

Federal district courts would get jurisdiction over class actions with more than $5 million in controversy where plaintiffs and defendants are from different states, and any single defendant could remove such a case to federal court without the consent of the other defendants.
Either side could immediately appeal a decision to certify or refuse to certify a class, and all discovery would stop while that appeal is pending.

analysis.who_pays: Plaintiffs' contingency lawyers, whose fee awards face new limits and whose cases can be pulled into federal court, delayed, or restructured. Consumers who rely on class actions for small-dollar claims bear the cost if their cases stall in federal court or fail certification, since the bill aggregates each member's claim to reach the $5 million threshold and lets any defendant force the move.

drawbacks.text: The automatic discovery stay during an appeal of a class certification order gives defendants a tool to delay a case for years; the bill text stops all discovery and other proceedings while the appeal is pending unless a court finds otherwise.

Because each class member's small claim is added together to clear the $5 million federal threshold, many ordinary consumer cases would be moved to federal court at the request of a single defendant, even over the objections of other plaintiffs.

The settlement protections only apply to cases in federal court, so they reach far fewer cases than the jurisdiction change does; the bill's consumer safeguards are narrower than its restructuring of where class actions are heard.

The House considered the bill under a rule that allowed only one hour of debate and specified which amendments could be offered, and the amendments from Reps. Jackson-Lee, Lofgren, and Sandlin all failed on recorded votes.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The settlement rules are genuine consumer protections: coupon-only deals and net-loss deals really did happen, and this bill requires a court to scrutinize them. But the centerpiece of the bill is the jurisdiction change, which shifts the battlefield to federal court where class actions are harder to win and where a single defendant can force the move. An honest weighing: class members get modest new protections at settlement, while companies get a much larger structural advantage before a case ever reaches settlement. The bill's defenders would say federal courts are more even-handed for nationwide cases; its critics would say it narrows consumers' practical ability to hold companies accountable for small-dollar harms.

outcome.mechanism: The House passed the bill in June 2003, but the Senate sent it to its Judiciary Committee and never voted on it before that Congress ended.

narrative.text: The House Judiciary Committee approved the bill 20-14 and reported it amended in June 2003.
The House passed the bill 253-170 on June 12, 2003, with 221 of 228 Republicans voting yes and 32 of 205 Democrats.
A Democratic motion to recommit the bill with instructions to change its effective date and strip the class-certification appeals provision failed 185-240.

The Senate received the bill on June 12, 2003, read it twice, and referred it to the Senate Judiciary Committee, where no further action was recorded before the 108th Congress ended on January 3, 2005.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the Senate never voted, large class actions stayed in state courts, which plaintiffs' lawyers preferred and corporate defendants did not; none of the bill's settlement restrictions or federal-jurisdiction rules took effect through this bill.

for.name: Rep. Bob Goodlatte
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and guided it through the House; it passed 253-170 on June 12, 2003.

for.name: House Republicans
for.what_they_did: Voted for final passage, supplying nearly all of the bill's 253 votes.

for.name: House Judiciary Committee
for.what_they_did: Held hearings, marked the bill up, and reported it amended 20-14 in June 2003.

for.name: 32 of 205 House Democrats
for.role: House Democrats who crossed party lines

for.name: U.S. Chamber of Commerce and business coalitions
for.what_they_did: Made class action reform a top legislative priority and pressed for the federal-jurisdiction change.

against.name: Rep. Anthony Weiner
against.what_they_did: Moved to recommit the bill with instructions to delay its effective date and strike the class-certification appeals provision; the motion failed 185-240.

against.name: Reps. Sheila Jackson-Lee, Zoe Lofgren, and Max Sandlin
against.what_they_did: Offered amendments on the floor; all failed on recorded votes.

against.name: Senate Judiciary Committee
against.role: Committee of referral (chaired by a Republican)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on June 12, 2003, and took no recorded action on it for the rest of the Congress.

against.name: Association of Trial Lawyers of America and consumer groups
against.what_they_did: Opposed moving class actions to federal court, arguing it would make it harder for consumers to recover for corporate wrongdoing.

sides.party_line_note: Final passage split mostly by party: 221 of 228 Republicans voted yes while 32 of 205 Democrats did; on the motion to recommit, 183 of 205 Democrats voted yes against 1 of 228 Republicans.

industries.industry: Corporate defendants (manufacturers, banks, insurers, drug makers facing class actions)
industries.note: The bill would let any single defendant move a large interstate class action into federal court, where certification is harder and an immediate appeal freezes discovery. That structural advantage comes directly out of consumers' practical ability to sue in the courts of their home states.

The bill caps the practices that produced large fees from coupon settlements and lets companies move cases to a federal forum. Trial lawyers legitimately align with class members in many cases, but the settlement-abuse provisions the bill targets were aimed at abuses by this industry.

The bill shifts a large new category of cases onto federal dockets and adds immediate appeals of certification orders, which supporters argued would produce more even-handed treatment of interstate cases and faster resolution.
